paper_title: Trajectory-Level Speculation with Semantic Verification for Tool-Using Agents

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Large language model agents solve tasks through long sequences of tool calls, and the prevailing design has a single strong model generate every step, although many steps are routine enough for a much smaller model. Existing ways of sharing this work keep the strong model as the generator: routers and collaborative agents decide which model handles each query or step, and speculative methods check a small model's drafts one step at a time, usually against the strong model's own action. We introduce SpecAgent, a collaboration protocol that turns the strong model from the author of each step into a reviewer of steps drafted by a weak model. The weak model executes read-only tool calls as it drafts, so that every step is grounded in real observations, and holds the first action that would modify the environment. The strong model then verifies the drafted segment in a single prefill pass, commits the longest prefix it judges semantically valid, and repairs the first rejected step. Because verification replaces autoregressive decoding with parallel prefill, the strong model decodes only short verdicts and occasional repairs rather than every step. On $τ^2$-Bench, SpecAgent comes within one point of the strong model's success rate while roughly halving memory traffic and wall time, and on AutomationBench and VitaBench it recovers 44-75% of the quality gap while lowering both. In an edge-cloud deployment on MCP-Atlas with three cloud models, it closes 53-75% of the weak-strong quality gap while the strong model generates at most half as many tokens. These results suggest that a strong model need not author every step of an agent: reviewing grounded drafts retains most of its quality while cutting both latency and memory traffic.

Introduction Language-model agents now solve tasks through long sequences of tool calls and user turns (Deng et al., 2026), from tens of turns in customer service to up to hundred in everyday life services  (Table 1)  . The prevailing design has one strong model generate every step, so serving cost grows with the length of the trajectory and is dominated by the strong models token-by-token decoding. Yet many steps are routine, such as looking up an order, reading record, or searching again, and much smaller model could often produce them. Table 1 Representative trajectory length per task for frontier agents, in turns (messages from the agent, the user, and tools). Real-World MCP Services (MCP-Atlas) Transactional Interaction (𝜏2-Bench) Business Workflows (AutomationBench) Life Services (VitaBench) 2030 turns 3080 turns 4060 turns 50100 turns Corresponding author(s): Yinhong Liu (yl535@cam.ac.uk), Zhijiang Guo (zhijiangguo@hkust-gz.edu.cn) 1 Trajectory-Level Speculation with Semantic Verification for Tool-Using Agents Existing ways of sharing this work keep the strong model as the generator. Routers pick one model per query (Aggarwal et al., 2024; Chen et al., 2023b; Ding et al., 2024; Ong et al., 2025), and collaborative agents decide, step by step, which model should act (Gao et al., 2026), so every step is still written by one model from scratch. Speculative agents carry the draft-and-verify idea of speculative decoding (Leviathan et al., 2023) over to actions (Hua et al., 2024; Ye et al., 2026), but usually keep draft only when it matches the strong models own action, so the strong model must still generate each reference step and its work is overlapped rather than removed. Recent variants replace matching with step-level critic (Huang et al., 2025; Zhong et al., 2026), but they check one predicted step at time in search-style tasks whose actions do not change the environment. Exact matching is also too strict for agents: different queries, lookup orders, or argument choices can all lead to valid solution (Liu et al., 2026), and progress that differs from the strong models choice is discarded. We therefore ask: can strong model review several steps drafted by weak model, and keep what is valid, instead of generating every step itself? We answer it with SpecAgent, in which small Weak model drafts the trajectory and large Strong model reviews it, separating acting from committing (Figure 1). Three properties of agents shape its design. First, draft is meaningful only if it is grounded, because later steps depend on what earlier tool calls return; the Weak model therefore executes read-only calls as it drafts. Second, some actions cannot be undone, so the Weak model holds the first state-changing action, such as changing an order, and the Strong model reviews the segment before it runs, commits the longest prefix it judges semantically valid, and repairs the first rejected step. Third, review must cost less than generation even though the reviewer reads the full context: the Strong model reads segment in one parallel prefill pass, whereas generating it would require decoding every token. We compare against Strong-only and Weak-only, the single-model agents in which one model generates every step, and evaluate complete qualityresource operating points, counting both models and keeping compute, memory traffic, and wall time as separate axes. On 𝜏2-Bench, SpecAgent comes within one point of Strong-only success while reducing estimated memory traffic to 4357% and wall time to 4154% of Strong-only; on AutomationBench and VitaBench it recovers 44% and 75% of the WeakStrong quality gap, again with lower memory traffic and wall time. In an edgecloud deployment on MCP-Atlas with three cloud Strong models, it closes 5375% of the gap while the Strong model generates at most half as many tokens. The saving comes from decoding rather than arithmetic: estimated FLOPs rise by 3038% on 𝜏2 and AutomationBench and by 87% on VitaBench, so SpecAgent suits memory-bandwidth-bound serving. Our contributions are as follows. Framework. SpecAgent, weakstrong protocol in which the Weak model drafts with real read-only tool calls and holds the first state-changing action, and the Strong model commits the longest prefix it judges semantically valid and repairs the first rejected step, together with cost model that predicts when replacing Strong decoding by prefill saves memory traffic and time. Evaluation. Experiments on 𝜏2-Bench, AutomationBench, VitaBench, and an edgecloud deployment on MCP-Atlas with three cloud Strong models, comparing complete qualityresource operating points against WeakStrong collaboration and speculative baselines. Analysis. An accounting of where the savings arise: measured Strong traffic and time follow the cost model, the saving comes from decoding, not computation, and it shrinks as acceptance falls. 2. Related Work Speculative execution. Speculative decoding lets small model draft tokens that large model verifies in parallel while preserving its output distribution (Chen et al., 2023a; Leviathan et al., 2023); Trajectory-Level Speculation with Semantic Verification for Tool-Using Agents Figure 1 (a) Strong-only agent generates every step by decoding. (b) SpecAgent lets the Weak model draft ahead, running reads at once and holding the first write. The Strong model reviews the draft in single prefill pass, keeps the valid steps, and replaces the rejected write; the Weak model then resumes. Bars indicate relative Strong-model memory reads. it is complementary to SpecAgent, accelerating each models own decoding. The draft-then-verify pattern has since been applied to reasoning and search (Fu et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2025a,b) and to agents, where fast model predicts plans, actions, or tool calls (Guan et al., 2025; Hooper et al., 2026; Hua et al., 2024; Ji et al., 2026; Nichols et al., 2025; Ye et al., 2026), sometimes with relaxed or semantic matching (Huang et al., 2025; Zhong et al., 2026). These methods target latency and keep draft when it agrees with the large models own step. SpecAgent instead verifies multi-step, grounded segments in one pass and checks only before actions that change the environment. Routing and weakstrong collaboration. Cascades and routers pick one model per query, including edgecloud deployments (Aggarwal et al., 2024; Chen et al., 2023b; Ding et al., 2024; Ong et al., 2025); agent-level methods hand control between models during trajectory (Gao et al., 2026; Hemadri et al., 2026; Wei et al., 2026). In both, the model in control generates each step; in SpecAgent, the Strong model decides how much drafted progress to keep and generates only repairs. Verification versus generation. Checking candidate is often easier than producing one, as verifiers and process reward models show for reasoning (Cobbe et al., 2021; Lightman et al., 2024). SpecAgent applies this asymmetry to agent trajectories, with the Strong model as the verifier, and exploits its cost counterpart: prefill processes many tokens per weight read, whereas decoding rereads them for every token (Kwon et al., 2023; Pope et al., 2023; Zheng et al., 2024). 3. This lets the Weak model speculate over whole stretches of the trajectory while keeping execution safe. When the Strong model steps in, it judges whether the drafted progress is valid rather than whether it matches what it would have done, so it reviews the trajectory instead of writing it (Figure 1). Experiments We evaluate SpecAgent on agent tasks that mix reads, state-changing actions, and user-visible replies. The experiments ask three questions. Q1: how much of the WeakStrong quality gap does semantic prefix verification recover? Q2: which resources does it save, and which does it not? Q3: how does it compare with existing WeakStrong collaboration methods at their own operating points? 4.1. Setup Benchmarks. 𝜏2-Bench Airline (50 tasks) and Retail (114 tasks) test multi-turn customer service against simulated user, mixing database reads, mutations, and replies (Barres et al., 2025). We run three independent trajectories per task and report the two domains separately because their action mix and difficulty differ. AutomationBench tests long business workflows whose success is checked on the final environment state (Shepard and Salimans, 2026); we aggregate its 600 public tasks into one block, with its development domain excluded, and run one trajectory per task. VitaBench Delivery (100 tasks) tests food-delivery service against simulated user, judged by an LLM against task rubrics (He et al., 2025); we run two trajectories per task. MCP-Atlas, run against real tool servers in an edgecloud deployment, is reported separately (Section 4.3). Models and methods. On 𝜏2, AutomationBench, and VitaBench, the Weak model is Qwen3.5-4B and the Strong model is Qwen3.5-397B-A17B (Qwen Team, 2026). Weak-only and Strong-only run the same agent loop with single model. AgentCollab (Gao et al., 2026), the WeakStrong collaboration baseline, escalates to Strong using its published self-evaluation signal. Speculative Actions (Ye et al., 2026) keeps Strong as the actor and speculates on upcoming steps to hide latency; we port the authors released agent to 𝜏2 (Appendix E). We do not port it to AutomationBench or VitaBench. All methods run on the same Weak and Strong deployments. SpecAgent reviews at state-changing actions with chunk size 𝐾 = 6 on 𝜏2 and VitaBench and 𝐾 = 8 on AutomationBench; other adapter settings and all prompts are listed in Appendix D. Serving. On 𝜏2, AutomationBench, and VitaBench, all models run on NVIDIA H20 GPUs: the Weak model on single GPU with SGLang (Zheng et al., 2024), and the Strong model with 16-way tensor parallelism. Every method runs eight tasks concurrently against the same deployments, so wall time is compared under common load. EdgeCloud Deployment: MCP-Atlas MCP-Atlas evaluates multi-step tool use against real Model Context Protocol servers for search, code execution, databases, and productivity tools (Anthropic, 2024; Bandi et al., 2026); an LLM judge scores each response by the share of reference claims it covers. Where to review: also holding replies, or reviewing every chunk including reads, more than triples the Strong calls and raises HBM-read by 6379% and wall time 2.53.0 (past Strong-only), while lowering Pass@1. Tools are classified as reads or writes from each benchmarks documentation and their observed effect on the environment, or, on VitaBench, from its own read/write tool labels. Rejecting read is logical de-commitment: the read is removed from the agents history and from what the Strong model reviews, but an external service may still keep traces of it, such as access logs. The guarantee is therefore that no action classified as state-changing executes before review, not that every effect of speculation is physically rolled back. On 𝜏2-Bench and VitaBench, replies to the simulated user cannot be undone but are not held: they leave the database unchanged, the users next turn returns as an observation, and on 𝜏2 holding them more than triples Strong calls without improving quality (Figure 4). On AutomationBench and MCP-Atlas the final message is the graded answer, so it is held like write, and on MCP-Atlas it is reviewed against the evidence gathered by earlier reads. MCP-Atlas and VitaBench tool outputs can be long, so tool results are truncated in the verifiers view (older ones only on MCP-Atlas). 𝐾 bounds how many reads accumulate before an unreviewed commit. You are the Strong trajectory reviewer for Weak-led customer-service agent in the "{domain}" domain. Notice ignored contradictions, mutations whose preconditions are unmet, replies that claim work that was not done, and unproductive repeats. 20 Trajectory-Level Speculation with Semantic Verification for Tool-Using Agents Customer-service replies: - Asking for user id, reservation id, date, or name that is not yet in the task, customer messages, or tool observations is justified continuation. Do not reject it for failing to finish the request. - reply that promises cancellation, refund, booking change, waiver, or other state change is commit. Reject it unless that mutation is already in confirmed_history or this chunk with successful observation. - When the policy requires explicit customer confirmation before acting, draft that mutates without that answer is unjustified. "The customer implied yes" is not confirmation. Policy: - mutation or denial is justified only by sentence in the domain policy above. If you cannot point to that sentence, do not invent rule. - If two policy-legal outcomes remain, do not reject the draft for picking one unless the conversation plus policy uniquely selects the other. Executed reads (pending=false lookups): - The observation is already real. Rejecting the read cannot undo it; it only discards later steps. Do not zeroor partial-accept reads-only prefix because later mutation would be better, because the agent is "still searching", or because the matching reservation has not turned up yet. Searching the customers existing reservations for the one they described is justified. - Reject an executed read only when the tool or required arguments are invalid: unknown tool, missing required argument, or an identifier that never appeared in the task, customer messages, or prior observations. Pending mutations (pending=true tool calls): - Judge the call as if it will run. Wrong user id, reservation id, payment id, amount, cabin, or date is reject even if later undo exists. 3. Repair. You are the Strong customer-service agent continuing from reviewed trajectory. Reassess the conversation and produce exactly one useful next step. You are invoked only when replacement_action was null or failed the schema guard; do not re-verify the retained prefix. 1. INPUT AND EVIDENCE - You receive the original task and tools, the retained dialogue, and review.reason. The retained dialogue is confirmed history plus the accepted prefix, with actions and original observations. - Treat the review as diagnosis to examine, not as new factual evidence. Check its material claims against retained observations; when they conflict, follow the observations. 2. CHOOSE ONE STEP - Reply when the required work for this customer turn is done, or when the policy requires asking the customer something you do not have. - Prefer missing lookup or required confirmation question over speculative mutation. - Otherwise issue one tool call targeting the blocking evidence gap or the policy-legal mutation whose preconditions are already met. - Follow the supplied schema. Do not invent identifiers. 3. OUTPUT Produce exactly one assistant step: either one tool call or one reply. Do not mention the reviewer, the discarded draft, or this protocol. E. Speculative Actions on 𝜏2-Bench Speculative Actions (Ye et al., 2026) targets latency rather than Strong-model work. An authoritative Actor produces every committed step, while faster Speculator predicts upcoming environment steps and executes them in advance. In the authors 𝜏-bench retail setting, the Speculator predicts the users next query and the API calls needed to answer it; the paper describes validating these guesses once the real query arrives and restricting speculative side effects to idempotent, reversible, or sandboxed actions, and it reports API-prediction accuracy rather than task success. We ported the authors released 𝜏-bench agent to 𝜏2-Bench with our model pair. The Strong model acts at every step. Whenever it replies to the user, the Weak model role-plays the next user message in the background, and Strong decider continues from that guess for up to five tool steps; the 22 Trajectory-Level Speculation with Semantic Verification for Tool-Using Agents resulting tool calls and observations are added to the context on the next user turn. As in the released code, these background tool calls execute in the live environment without read-only filter, and their results are added without checking the guess against the real user message. This configuration reached 72.0% Pass@1 on Airline and 48.5% on Retail, below Weak-only (80.0% and 80.4%), while issuing 17.4 and 17.1 Strong calls per trajectory, more than Strong-only (13.8 and 13.1). The extra Strong calls come from the background decider, which runs on top of the Strong actor. Because background calls may change environment state and add observations on the basis of guessed user message, the released implementation is not lossless in this setting, which plausibly explains part of the quality drop; we did not diagnose it further. These numbers therefore characterize the released implementation rather than the guarded design described in the paper.
